column1: @jakebailey I believe I know why this happens. Here is a demonstration:
When esbuild sees a file without any exports
column2: it attempts to guess what type of module it is. That logic lives [here](https://github.com/evanw/esbuild/blob/4e11b50fe3178ed0a78c077df78788d66304d379/internal/js_parser/js_parser.go#L17641-L17660):

column1: // If this module has no exports
column2: try to determine what kind of module it

column1: // is by looking at node's ""type"" field in ""package.json"" and/or whether
// "".cjs"" or "".cts"" or (""type: commonjs"" and ("".js"" or "".jsx"" or "".ts"" or "".tsx""))
// "".mjs"" or "".mts"" or (""type: module"" and ("".js"" or "".jsx"" or "".ts"" or "".tsx""))
// Treat unknown modules containing an import statement as ESM. Otherwise
// the bundler will treat this file as CommonJS if it's imported and ESM
The file `src/deprecatedCompat/5.0/identifierProperties.ts` has no exports (there may be others too
column2: but I haven't checked). In that case the file is considered to be a CommonJS module if `type: commonjs` is present in `package.json`
column3: which means that imports of that file use `require()`
column4: which means that re-exports of that file use dynamic re-exports via a property-copying loop instead of static re-exports via inheriting the re-exported properties at compile time
column5: which results in a bigger bundle size.

column1: If `type` is absent then esbuild guesses that the file should be considered ESM if there is an `import` statement
column2: which there is in `src/deprecatedCompat/5.0/identifierProperties.ts`. It's true that node would default to CommonJS in this case
column3: but esbuild can't really do that because esbuild is a bundler and bundling code that people would consider to be ESM as CommonJS instead by default can result in much worse code
column4: which is a non-starter. So esbuild only does that if you explicitly say that files without `.m*` or `.c*` extensions should be CommonJS.

column2: so to recap for my own understanding
column3: for files without exports
column4: setting `type=commonjs` forced us into the first case
column5: rather than falling back to the default. I'm honestly surprised that just having an import statement wouldn't be enough to force it into ESM (for ""maximum good codegen"")
column6: but I know this stuff is fickle. In our case
column7: we kinda do want it to treat everything as ESM; with the way our build works
column8: we actually `--define` away `require` entirely and replace it post-build
column9: making the entire bundle entirely ESM internally (source wise)
column10: only calling `require` on Node. Probably we're unique in that we don't have external deps whatsoever.

column1: This code offers coordination beyond what a plain `sync.Mutex` lock/unlock can provide. It implements a form of *serialized critical section with wait-for-completion*
column2: allowing concurrent goroutines to *queue up* and wait for prior operations to finish **without racing** or **starving**. Here's what makes it preferable to just using `ep.Lock()` and `ep.Unlock()`:

column1: Suppose multiple goroutines want to perform mutually exclusive ""join"" or ""leave"" operations on the same `endpoint`. A simple `mutex` would protect concurrent access
column2: but it doesn't **serialize overlapping attempts** that *wait* for others to finish cleanly.

column1: * **block entirely** until the lock is released
* and wouldn't know **when the previous operation completed**
column2: only when it *released the lock*.

column1: Thatâs fine *if* the operation finishes instantly and there are no coordination needs. But here we need stronger semantics: **no two join/leave ops can overlap**
column2: and new ones must **wait until the previous one has finished**
column3: not just until the lock is free.

column1: * If a join/leave is already in progress (`ep.joinLeaveDone != nil`)
column2: the function:

column1: * waits for the current join/leave to signal completion (via `<-joinLeaveDone`)
This prevents overlapping execution of `joinLeaveStart()`s in a *cooperative*
column2: race-free way.
it blocks on a channel: efficient
column3: non-CPU-hogging.

column1: * The `joinLeaveEnd()` method safely closes the channel
column2: waking all waiting goroutines that are blocked in `joinLeaveStart()`.

column1: * The pattern of releasing the lock *before* blocking on the channel avoids holding the mutex while waiting
column2: which would deadlock other operations trying to signal completion.

column1: ### ð Why not just a mutex?
Using only a mutex can't express this protocol:
* You canât wait on a previous operation's *completion* if all you have is `Lock/Unlock`.
* You'd have to build another layer anyway â like this â to wait for other goroutines to finish serialized operations.
Think of it like a ticket system for an exclusive operation:
* Only one person can ""do"" the thing at a time.

column2: they create a new ticket (channel) for the next in line to wait on.

column1: This code enables **safe queuing and completion signaling** for serialized operations (like join/leave) that canât run concurrently. A plain mutex doesnât provide that
